contraindications: Ampicillin and other penicillins: documented penicillin allergy (rash); Listeria cover with co-trimoxazole instead.
interactions: Trimethoprim with metformin: trimethoprim reduces renal tubular secretion of metformin and raises its level; withhold metformin.
Co-trimoxazole: raises serum potassium and creatinine; monitor potassium and renal function daily.
Dexamethasone with metformin: corticosteroid-induced hyperglycaemia (admission glucose 184 mg/dL); monitor capillary glucose and use insulin.

Ibuprofen: avoid with platelets 95 x10^3/uL, coagulopathy and septic shock.
Co-trimoxazole can lower the platelet count further: monitor platelets with the DIC panel (platelets 95 x10^3/uL).

prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.

Do not delay lumbar puncture or antibiotics to obtain a CT head: cranial imaging is not routine before lumbar puncture (WHO 2025 section A.4; NICE NG240 1.4.6) and no imaging-first criterion is present.
Do not give ampicillin or another penicillin: documented penicillin allergy (rash).
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
required_recommendations: Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.

Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion, after blood cultures and without waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.4.1 and 1.6.3); the non-severe penicillin rash is not a contraindication. Add vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance to penicillin or third-generation cephalosporins is highly prevalent locally (WHO 2025, conditional recommendation).

Add co-trimoxazole IV (trimethoprim component 10 to 20 mg/kg per day in divided doses every 6 to 12 hours) for Listeria monocytogenes cover because of diabetes mellitus, in place of ampicillin given the penicillin allergy (NICE NG240).

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3). Continue for 4 days: Streptococcus pneumoniae is identified.

Treat as septic shock with overt DIC: fluid resuscitation and vasopressors to a mean arterial pressure of at least 65 mmHg, serial platelets, fibrinogen, INR and D-dimer with replacement for bleeding or procedures, serial mapping of purpura, and assess for adrenal haemorrhage (Waterhouse-Friderichsen) if shock persists.

Proceed to lumbar puncture without prior cranial imaging: no WHO 2025 section A.4 criterion is present (GCS 13, no focal signs, no cranial nerve deficit, no papilloedema, no new seizure, not severely immunocompromised). Age, confusion and diabetes are not imaging criteria. Stabilise the shock and correct the coagulopathy first (WHO 2025 A.1.1; NICE NG240 1.4.11): the lumbar puncture follows resuscitation, and antibiotics are not delayed for it.
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose with paired blood glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP.

Narrow therapy once the organism and susceptibilities are known: continue ceftriaxone for Streptococcus pneumoniae (ceftriaxone MIC 0.5 mg/L or less, susceptible by CLSI meningitis breakpoints) and stop co-trimoxazole.

Neurosurgical review for the ventriculitis and communicating ventriculomegaly, with repeat imaging if consciousness falls; external ventricular drainage only for symptomatic or progressive hydrocephalus.
ENT assessment of the cochlear implant and of the paranasal sinuses as portals of entry.
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.
After recovery, complete pneumococcal vaccination for the cochlear implant (he has received PCV13 only), for example a dose of PCV20 or PCV21 per the national schedule.
Arrange formal audiological assessment before discharge, or within 4 weeks of discharge if it cannot be done before (WHO 2025, strong recommendation). Include the left ear and the implant's function.

avoided_actions.rationale: ECG does not contribute to the diagnosis or acute management of bacterial meningitis.
No evidence of endocarditis as a primary source in this case; echocardiography is not part of routine meningitis workup.
No arrhythmia indication; continuous cardiac monitoring contributes nothing to meningitis diagnosis or treatment.
PET imaging has no role in acute meningitis diagnosis; CT and MRI cover the indications.
Amyloid PET is a dementia biomarker tool with no role in acute infectious meningitis.

accepted: Acute bacterial meningitis due to Streptococcus pneumoniae with ventriculitis

differential.diagnosis: Meningococcal disease (meningococcal sepsis with or without meningitis)
differential.key_features: Petechial rash on the trunk and legs with fever, meningism and shock makes it the first concern at the bedside and drives droplet precautions and immediate empirical therapy; N. meningitidis is not detected on CSF PCR and S. pneumoniae grows from blood and CSF, so the rash reflects DIC in pneumococcal sepsis.
Excluded: neutrophilic CSF (3840 cells/uL, 94% neutrophils), glucose ratio 0.06, Gram-positive diplococci and S. pneumoniae on PCR; viral targets not detected.
No seizures or focal deficit; HSV-1 and HSV-2 not detected; pyogenic CSF; no temporal parenchymal change on MRI.
Implant and sinus portals make it a complication to exclude; MRI shows no empyema or abscess.
Excluded: hyperacute course, neutrophilic CSF and S. pneumoniae identified.
Headache built up with fever over hours; no hemorrhage on CT or MRI; purulent CSF.

key_clinical_evidence: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotics are given within 60 minutes of suspicion; neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay them (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.1).

Proceed to lumbar puncture without prior cranial imaging: no WHO 2025 section A.4 criterion is present (GCS 13, no focal signs, no cranial nerve deficit, no papilloedema, no new seizure, not severely immunocompromised). Age, confusion and diabetes are not imaging criteria. Stabilise the shock and correct the coagulopathy first (WHO 2025 A.1.1; NICE NG240 1.4.11): the lumbar puncture follows resuscitation, and antibiotics are not delayed for it.

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3).

A negative Gram stain does not exclude bacterial meningitis: sensitivity is about 85% with wide confidence limits (WHO 2025), lower after antibiotics; culture and multiplex PCR establish the organism.
A CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.4 or less is abnormally low (WHO 2025 A.2.2) and is more informative than the absolute value, above all in hyperglycaemia.

Empirical therapy is ceftriaxone or cefotaxime within 60 minutes, with ampicillin when a Listeria risk factor (age over 60, pregnancy, immunocompromise) is present; vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance is locally prevalent (WHO 2025).

Ependymal enhancement, intraventricular debris, and restricted diffusion in the ventricular system indicate ventriculitis, which prolongs treatment and calls for neurosurgical review if hydrocephalus progresses.

Hypotension, lactate 4.4 mmol/L, platelets 95, INR 1.5, D-dimer 6.2 ug/mL FEU and a falling fibrinogen (139 mg/dL, where an acute-phase response would raise it) with a petechial rash indicate septic shock with overt DIC (ISTH overt-DIC score 5).
Cochlear implants are a recognised risk factor for pneumococcal meningitis; a non-severe penicillin rash does not preclude ceftriaxone, but Listeria cover then uses co-trimoxazole.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Petechiae with fever and meningism make meningococcal disease the first bedside concern and justify droplet precautions and immediate therapy, but here they reflect DIC in pneumococcal sepsis: N. meningitidis is not detected and S. pneumoniae grows from blood and CSF.
red_herrings.data_point: Petechial rash on the trunk and proximal lower extremities
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on meningococcal disease and overlook the cochlear implant and sinus portals of a pneumococcal infection.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Parameningeal sinus disease can be a SOURCE of pneumococcal meningitis, not an alternative diagnosis; the CSF profile remains the deciding evidence.
red_herrings.data_point: Maxillary and ethmoid sinus opacification on CT after a recent purulent rhinorrhoea
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest uncomplicated sinusitis as the source of headache and fever, deferring meningitis evaluation.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Cochlear implants are an established portal for pneumococcal CSF entry; ENT involvement and device assessment are indicated alongside antibiotic therapy.

red_herrings.intended_effect: May be overlooked as a portal of entry for pneumococcal meningitis.

metadata.clinical_notes: Pneumococcal meningitis with ventriculitis in a patient with a cochlear implant and chronic sinusitis, complicated by septic shock and DIC.
key_teaching_points: Cochlear implants confer increased risk of pneumococcal meningitis
Do not delay antibiotics for any reason in suspected bacterial meningitis
Adjunctive dexamethasone is most beneficial in pneumococcal meningitis
Hearing loss screening is mandatory in meningitis survivors

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Ramirez is a 38-year-old right-handed man who presents to the emergency department via ambulance after his wife called 911 when she found him confused and febrile at home. According to his wife, the patient was in his usual state of health until approximately 18 hours ago when he began complaining of a severe, progressively worsening headache, initially starting at the back of his head and then becoming diffuse. He took ibuprofen 400 mg twice without relief. By yesterday evening he developed chills and his wife measured a temperature of 39.2 degrees Celsius at home. He vomited three times overnight and complained that the bedroom lights were too bright, pulling a pillow over his face. His wife noted that around 4 AM, approximately 10 hours before presentation, he began having difficulty following conversation, giving nonsensical answers to simple questions, and appeared to not know where he was. She attempted to give him more ibuprofen and water but he was unable to keep anything down. He had a recent upper respiratory tract infection approximately one week ago with nasal congestion and purulent rhinorrhea, for which he did not seek medical attention. He has a history of a right cochlear implant. His wife also reports that she noticed a rash of small reddish-purple spots on his chest and legs that developed overnight. He has not had any seizures, and there is no history of recent travel, tick exposure, or contact with anyone known to have meningitis. He received the pneumococcal vaccine (PCV13) at the time of cochlear implant placement 4 years ago but has not received a booster or PPSV23.

neurological_exam.additional: Marked neck stiffness with resistance to passive flexion. Positive Kernig sign bilaterally — resistance and pain with passive knee extension when hip is flexed to 90 degrees. Positive Brudzinski sign — involuntary hip and knee flexion with passive neck flexion. Petechial rash noted on trunk and proximal lower extremities. No tongue bite marks. No evidence of trauma.
neurological_exam.coordination: Unable to perform finger-to-nose or heel-to-shin testing reliably due to altered mental status and poor cooperation.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: CN II: Pupils equal at 3 mm, sluggishly reactive to light bilaterally. Visual fields unable to assess reliably. Fundoscopy limited by photophobia; no papilledema seen on the views obtained. CN III/IV/VI: Extraocular movements grossly conjugate, no obvious gaze deviation. CN V: Withdraws to light touch bilaterally. CN VII: Face symmetric at rest, grimaces symmetrically to noxious stimulation. CN VIII: Hearing grossly intact on left to voice; cochlear implant on right. CN IX/X: Gag reflex present bilaterally. CN XI: Not reliably assessed. CN XII: Tongue midline when protruded on command.
neurological_exam.gait: Not assessed; patient unable to stand due to altered consciousness and severe headache.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Somnolent, arousable to voice but drifts back to sleep. Glasgow Coma Scale 13 (E3 V4 M6). Oriented to person only; unable to state location or date. Speech is slow and dysarthric. Unable to sustain attention for serial sevens. Follows simple one-step commands intermittently. Unable to assess recall reliably due to altered sensorium.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Tone mildly increased in all four extremities. Moves all extremities spontaneously and to command, though slowly. Strength approximately 4/5 throughout upper and lower extremities bilaterally, limited by poor cooperation. No clear focal weakness. No pronator drift assessable given mental status.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 3+ bilaterally, triceps 3+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 3+ bilaterally, patellar 3+ bilaterally, Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Bilateral plantar responses are extensor (upgoing Babinski signs).
neurological_exam.sensory: Withdraws to painful stimuli symmetrically in all four extremities. Light touch grossly intact bilaterally. Detailed sensory examination deferred due to altered mental status.
